subsection: 4. Case study: the Treaty negotiations, October–December 1921

notes.b: The Truce of 11 July 1921 ended open fighting and opened talks between the British government and the Irish leaders. The question was what status Ireland would hold within the British Empire.
points: Lloyd George invited de Valera to a conference in a letter of 24 June 1921, and the Truce took effect on 11 July 1921.

De Valera and Lloyd George met in July 1921 and failed to agree; de Valera proposed ‘external association’, under which Ireland would be a separate nation linked to Britain by a common allegiance to the Crown.
Lloyd George rejected external association because it would leave Ireland outside the Empire's structure; his government wanted dominion status, as held by Canada and Australia.
De Valera decided to stay in Dublin as President of Dáil Éireann and did not lead the Irish delegation, believing that a president should not take a subordinate role in negotiations.
The Irish delegation was formed by the Dáil Cabinet and consisted of plenipotentiaries with authority to negotiate, but not to sign a final treaty without referring back to the Cabinet.
British war-weariness, the cost of the Irish campaign and the threat to Britain's international position after the 1921 Washington naval talks all pushed the government towards a settlement.

notes.b: The Irish side was led by Arthur Griffith, who had founded Sinn Féin, and Michael Collins, the IRA's intelligence chief. The British side was led by Lloyd George with a strong cabinet team.
points: The Irish plenipotentiaries were Arthur Griffith, Michael Collins, Robert Barton, George Gavan Duffy and Éamonn Duggan, with Erskine Childers as their secretary.
The Irish delegation was based at Hans Place in London, away from the official talks at Downing Street, and worked out its positions in private meetings.
The British team was led by Lloyd George, with Lord Birkenhead, Winston Churchill, Austen Chamberlain, Hamar Greenwood and Sir Laming Worthington-Evans among its members.
Griffith was the chief Irish negotiator and Collins was the decisive voice on the military and security questions; both were under pressure from the Dáil cabinet and from their own supporters.
The British insisted that the Irish delegates were negotiating on behalf of Irish opinion and were not the representatives of a sovereign state, a dispute over status that ran through the talks.

notes.b: The talks turned on five questions: the oath to the Crown, the position of Northern Ireland and the Boundary Commission, the treaty ports, defence, and finance.
points: The oath to the Crown: the Irish delegates were asked to swear allegiance to the King, and the oath was the most difficult issue for the Irish republicans in Dublin.
Northern Ireland: the British offered a Boundary Commission to adjust the border, and the Irish side accepted it while the British kept Northern Ireland's right to opt out.
Treaty ports: Britain demanded the retention of the naval ports at Berehaven, Queenstown (Cobh) and Lough Swilly, which the Irish delegates saw as a threat to sovereignty.
Defence: the British wanted control of coastal defence and the Irish were pressed to accept a limited army, with British interests protected.
Finance: the Irish negotiators disputed how much of the British national debt the Irish state would take on and how the land annuities owed by Irish tenant farmers would be treated.

notes.h: Key moments and the signing, October–December 1921
notes.b: The talks ran for about two months and came to a crisis in early December, when Lloyd George issued an ultimatum that the delegates accepted under pressure.
points: The formal conference began in October 1921, with the Irish delegates first presenting their case for a republic and then moving towards dominion status.
Griffith kept private channels open with the British during the deadlock, and the Boundary Commission was one of the points on which the two sides kept talking.
On 5 December 1921 Lloyd George told the Irish delegates that if they refused he would wage ‘immediate and terrible war’ on Ireland; the threat was delivered in a final meeting.
The Irish delegates signed the Anglo-Irish Treaty in the early hours of 6 December 1921 at 10 Downing Street, without the Dáil cabinet's formal consent.
Griffith and Collins signed in the belief that the terms were the best available under threat, while de Valera and his supporters objected that the delegates had exceeded their powers.

notes.b: The Treaty created the Irish Free State as a dominion within the British Empire. It gave a measure of self-government but kept the link with the Crown and the partition of Ireland.
points: The Irish Free State was given dominion status on the model of Canada, with its own parliament and a government responsible to the Dáil.
Members of parliament and the Free State's officials had to take an oath of allegiance to the King, and a Governor-General represented the Crown in Dublin.
Northern Ireland could opt out of the Free State, and a Boundary Commission was to adjust the border between the two states.
Britain kept three treaty ports, Berehaven, Queenstown and Lough Swilly, for its naval use.
The Free State agreed to take a share of the British national debt, and the question of land annuities was left to later negotiation.

notes.h: Outcomes: Dáil ratification and the split, January 1922
notes.b: The Dáil debated the Treaty for about two weeks in late 1921 and early 1922. Its ratification split the republican movement and led directly to the Civil War.
points: The Dáil debated the Treaty from 14 December 1921, and on 7 January 1922 it ratified the Treaty by 64 votes to 57.
De Valera resigned as President of the Dáil and led the anti-Treaty side, which argued that the delegates had betrayed the republic.
Griffith became President of Dáil Éireann in January 1922, and Collins became chairman of the Provisional Government on 14 January 1922.
Collins described the Treaty as a ‘stepping stone’ to a fuller freedom, a phrase that became a central argument of the pro-Treaty side.
The IRA split between pro-Treaty and anti-Treaty factions, and the two sides occupied rival positions across Dublin and the country, leading to the Civil War from June 1922.

notes.b: The Treaty's supporters and opponents both claimed it expressed the will of the Irish people, and historians still disagree about whether it was a realistic compromise or a betrayal.
points: Pro-Treaty argument: the Treaty gave the Free State control of its own affairs and a platform from which the republic could later be achieved.
Anti-Treaty argument: the oath to the King, the partition of Ireland and the treaty ports made the Treaty a betrayal of the 1916 proclamation and the 1919 Declaration of Independence.
De Valera's alternative proposals, such as his Document No. 2 of 1921, suggested an external association model that the British government refused.
Contemporary British opinion saw the Treaty as a successful end to the war, while many unionists in the north saw it as a threat to their position.
Historians differ over whether the British offered the best settlement available or whether the Irish delegates should have held out for a republic.
The Treaty's terms were revised by the Free State's constitution and by the external relations changes of the 1930s, which removed much of what the Treaty had imposed.

notes.h: Assessment: the Treaty negotiations, achievements and limits
notes.b: The negotiations achieved a state with real self-government, but at the cost of the republic, the oath and the partition of Ireland. Judgements depend on whether one measures the outcome against the republican ideal or against the realistic options of 1921.
points: Achievement: the Treaty ended the War of Independence and gave the Irish state dominion status with its own parliament, army and civil service.
Limit: the Treaty kept the oath to the King, the treaty ports and the partition of the island, which republicans regarded as unacceptable.
Contemporary view: many Irish voters and the Dáil majority accepted the Treaty as the best result that could be won under threat of war.
Later view: historians differ on whether Collins and Griffith overreached their powers, and on whether de Valera's stance made a settlement more difficult.
The Treaty negotiations shaped Irish politics for decades, because the question of its status divided the republican movement and the state's first governments.

keyTerms.definition: The status of a self-governing member of the British Empire, such as Canada, with its own parliament and a link to the Crown through a Governor-General.
The formal loyalty owed to the Crown, which the Treaty required members of the Free State's parliament and officials to swear.
Supreme authority over a state's own affairs, which the Treaty qualified by keeping the Crown, partition and the treaty ports.
De Valera's proposal that Ireland be a separate nation linked to Britain only through a shared Crown, which the British government rejected.
A negotiator with full authority to conduct talks and sign an agreement on behalf of a government.
The naval bases at Berehaven, Queenstown and Lough Swilly that Britain kept under the Treaty for its own use.
The body provided for in the Treaty to adjust the border between Northern Ireland and the Free State.
The Dáil's vote of 7 January 1922, by 64 to 57, to accept the Treaty, which split the republican movement.
The oath to the King that members of the Free State's parliament were required to take under the Treaty.
The Irish Free State, the dominion established by the Treaty of 1921, covering twenty-six counties of Ireland.
